subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the equation of locus of the point which is equidistant from A(2, 0) and the y-axis.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), chapter 1 LOCUS, Short Answer question 10(ii), book p.136. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a chapter-level marks banner over this section but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split 1+1+2 gives its first mark to the one move that decides this question — writing the distance from P to the y-axis as |x| — then one for the substitution, and the remaining two for the cancellation of x² that leaves a parabola. The unmarked opening step names the moving point and carries no mark of its own. Answer cross-checked by substituting the point (2, 2), which is 2 units from A(2, 0) and 2 units from the y-axis, and which satisfies the final equation. Paper position: Maths-1B Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say how far P is from the y-axis, and name the shape the locus turns out to be.

steps.label: Take the locus point
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Here one of the two things P is measured from is a LINE, not a point — the y-axis. That single difference is what makes this question a parabola instead of a circle.
steps.memory_tip: One measurement is to a point and one is to a LINE — that pairing always gives a parabola.
lines: Let P = (x, y) be a point on the locus.
Given point A = (2, 0). The y-axis is x = 0.

recall.must_convey: That the moving point is named P = (x, y), with the fixed point A(2, 0) and the fixed line x = 0.
accept: let P be x comma y
take the locus point as P x y
one is a point and the other is the y axis
locus point ni P x y ga teesukovali
the y axis is the line x equals zero

steps.why: Writing the y-axis as x = 0 makes it clear that the second distance is measured to a line, which is a different formula from the distance between two points.
common_mistakes: Measuring to the x-axis instead of the y-axis.
Giving the moving point fixed numbers instead of (x, y).

steps.label: Write the given condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The distance from P(x, y) to the y-axis is |x|, not |y| — it is the sideways gap. Squaring removes the modulus bars.
steps.memory_tip: Distance to the y-axis is |x|, the sideways gap. Squaring removes the modulus bars.
lines: Distance from P to the y-axis = |x|

recall.must_convey: That the distance from P to the y-axis is |x|, so the condition is PA = |x| and PA² = x².
accept: the distance from P to the y axis is mod x
P A equals mod x so P A squared equals x squared
squaring removes the modulus
y axis nunchi distance mod x avuthundi
the perpendicular distance to the y axis is the x coordinate

steps.why: Squaring is what lets the modulus be dropped safely: |x|² and x² are the same number for every real x, so nothing is lost or added.
common_mistakes: Using |y| for the distance to the y-axis.
Dropping the modulus bars before squaring.

steps.label: Substitute the distance
steps.margin_note: Second mark. A(2, 0) has y-coordinate 0, so the second bracket is (y − 0)², which is simply y².
steps.memory_tip: A sits on the x-axis, so its y bracket is (y − 0)², which is just y².

recall.must_convey: That the squared distance PA is written as (x − 2)² + y² and set equal to x².
accept: x minus two whole squared plus y squared equals x squared
substitute the distance formula on the left and x squared on the right
expand x minus two whole squared
distance formula substitute chesi expand cheyyali
the y bracket is just y squared

steps.why: Both sides now carry an x² term, which is the setting for the cancellation that turns this from a second-degree curve in both variables into a parabola.
common_mistakes: Writing (x + 2)² for a fixed x-coordinate of +2.

steps.label: Simplify to the locus
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. The x² cancels on both sides, so no x² survives — the locus is a parabola, y² = 4(x − 1), with vertex (1, 0). Check: (2, 2) is 2 units from A and 2 units from the y-axis, and satisfies this equation.
steps.memory_tip: The x² cancels across the equals sign, so y² survives alone — that is the parabola.

recall.must_convey: That x² cancels on both sides, leaving y² − 4x + 4 = 0, a parabola.
accept: the x squared cancels on both sides
we are left with y squared minus four x plus four equals zero
it can also be written as y squared equals four into x minus one
x square cancel avuthundi so parabola vasthundi
the locus is a parabola

steps.why: Only one of the two squared terms survives, so the curve is a parabola. The form y² = 4(x − 1) reads off the vertex (1, 0) directly, which is the midpoint of A and its foot on the y-axis.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the x² and also cancelling the −4x with it.
Writing y² = 4(x + 1) by taking the 4 across with the wrong sign.
